chapterTitle: Let All That You Do Be Done in Love — Giving, Open Doors, Faithful Workers and Maranatha
themeTitle: “After Fifteen Chapters of Correction, the Last Word Is Love”

scripture.text: Now concerning the collection for the saints, as I commanded the assemblies of Galatia, you do likewise.
scripture.understanding: “Now concerning” — the fifth topic from their letter: the λογεία, the collection, for the saints — the poor believers in Jerusalem (Romans 15:26). Paul had διατάσσω — given directions — to the churches of Galatia, and now gives the same to Corinth. Notice how the letter moves straight from the resurrection to fundraising. Because Christ is risen and your labour is not in vain (15:58), your money matters too.

scripture.text: On the first day of the week, let each one of you save, as he may prosper, that no collections be made when I come.
scripture.understanding: “On the first day of the week” — κατὰ μίαν σαββάτου, every first day after the Sabbath. This is one of the earliest pieces of evidence that Christians gathered on Sunday, the day of the resurrection (compare Acts 20:7). Each one is to τίθημι — set aside — and θησαυρίζω — store up, treasure — as he εὐοδόω, prospers, literally “is helped along the road.” Giving was to be regular, personal, proportional and planned. Not a last-minute emotional appeal when the apostle arrives.

scripture.text: When I arrive, I will send whoever you approve with letters to carry your gracious gift to Jerusalem.
scripture.understanding: Paul will not handle the money himself. The Corinthians will δοκιμάζω — test, approve — trustworthy people of their own choosing, and Paul will send them with ἐπιστολαί, letters of introduction, to ἀποφέρω — carry — their χάρις to Jerusalem. Notice the word: the gift is called “grace.” Financial integrity and transparency are part of gospel ministry (compare 2 Corinthians 8:20–21).

scripture.text: If it is appropriate for me to go also, they will go with me.
scripture.understanding: If it seems ἄξιος — fitting — for Paul to go too, the delegates will travel with him. In the end he did go, and Acts 24:17 records him telling the governor Felix that he had come to Jerusalem “to bring gifts for the needy to my nation.”

scripture.text: But I will come to you when I have passed through Macedonia, for I am passing through Macedonia.
scripture.understanding: Paul's travel plans. He will come to Corinth after διέρχομαι — passing through — Μακεδονία. These are the plans that later changed, prompting the Corinthians' charge of fickleness that Paul answers in 2 Corinthians 1:15–24.

scripture.text: But with you it may be that I will stay, or even winter, that you may send me on my journey wherever I go.
scripture.understanding: He may παραμένω — stay on — with them, perhaps even through the winter, when sea travel effectively stopped in the Mediterranean. And then they can προπέμπω — send him on his way, equip him for the next journey. Sending missionaries well was a recognised Christian duty (3 John 6).

scripture.text: For I do not wish to see you now in passing, but I hope to stay a while with you, if the Lord permits.
scripture.understanding: He does not want to see them only ἐν παρόδῳ — in passing. He hopes to stay a while “if the Lord permits.” Every plan in this chapter is held under the Lord's sovereignty (compare James 4:13–15).

scripture.text: But I will stay at Ephesus until Pentecost,
scripture.understanding: Paul is writing from Ephesus, and will stay there until πεντηκοστή — Pentecost, the fiftieth day after Passover. This, together with the Passover imagery of 5:7–8, suggests he may have been writing in the spring.

scripture.text: for a great and effective door has opened to me, and there are many adversaries.
scripture.understanding: Why stay? “A great and effective θύρα has ἀνοίγω — has been opened — to me.” A door is Paul's regular image for an opportunity for the gospel (2 Corinthians 2:12; Colossians 4:3). Μεγάλη καὶ ἐνεργής — great and effective, active, operative. “And there are many ἀντικείμενοι — adversaries, people lying in opposition.” Notice the “and”: the open door and the opposition came together. Opposition is not proof the door is closed. It is often proof that it is open.

scripture.text: Now if Timothy comes, see that he is with you without fear, for he does the work of the Lord, as I also do.
scripture.understanding: Timothy may arrive. “See that he is with you ἀφόβως — without fear.” Timothy was young and apparently timid by temperament (compare 1 Timothy 4:12; 2 Timothy 1:7), and Corinth was an intimidating church. Paul protects him: he does the ἔργον of the Lord, “as I also do.” A young worker doing the Lord's work deserves the same respect as the apostle.

scripture.text: Therefore let no one despise him. But set him forward on his journey in peace, that he may come to me; for I expect him with the brothers.
scripture.understanding: Μή τις αὐτὸν ἐξουθενήσῃ — let no one despise him, treat him as nothing; the word of 1:28. Instead προπέμπω — send him on — ἐν εἰρήνῃ, in peace, so that he can return to Paul. Paul knew how Corinth could treat a speaker it did not find impressive.

scripture.text: Now concerning Apollos, the brother, I strongly urged him to come to you with the brothers; and it was not at all his desire to come now; but he will come when he has an opportunity.
scripture.understanding: “Now concerning Apollos” — the sixth and last “now concerning.” The Corinthians had apparently asked for Apollos to come. Paul πολλὰ παρεκάλεσα — urged him strongly — to go. Apollos was not willing at that time, but will come when he has εὐκαιρία, an opportunity. This tiny verse destroys the idea that Paul and Apollos were rivals. Paul wanted the man some Corinthians preferred to him to go to them. And Apollos, perhaps wisely, did not want to feed the faction that bore his name.

scripture.text: Watch! Stand firm in the faith! Be courageous! Be strong!
scripture.understanding: Four military commands in rapid succession, like a commander's final orders before battle. Γρηγορεῖτε — stay awake, be on watch; the word of Jesus in Gethsemane (Matthew 26:41). Στήκετε ἐν τῇ πίστει — stand firm in the faith; hold your position. Ἀνδρίζεσθε — act like men, be courageous; the word appears in the Greek Old Testament's “be strong and courageous” to Joshua (Joshua 1). Κραταιοῦσθε — be strong, be strengthened. The Corinthians, who were proud and divided, needed courage and stability, not more spectacle.

scripture.text: Let all that you do be done in love.
scripture.understanding: And immediately the balancing command: πάντα ὑμῶν ἐν ἀγάπῃ γινέσθω — let everything you do happen in love. Courage without love becomes harshness; strength without love becomes domination. This one verse is the summary of the whole letter: factions, lawsuits, marriage, food, worship, gifts — all of it must be done in love. It is 1 Corinthians 13 compressed into eight words.

scripture.text: Now I beg you, brothers (you know the house of Stephanas, that it is the first fruits of Achaia, and that they have set themselves to serve the saints),
scripture.understanding: The household of Stephanas — the first converts in Achaia, ἀπαρχή, “first fruits,” the word of 15:20 — had ἑαυτοὺς ἔταξαν — appointed themselves, devoted themselves — to the διακονία, the service, of the saints. Nobody appointed them to a position; they took up the towel. Paul baptized this household himself (1:16).

scripture.text: that you also be in subjection to such, and to everyone who helps in the work and labors.
scripture.understanding: Paul asks the church to ὑποτάσσω — be subject — to such people, and to everyone who συνεργέω — works together — and κοπιάω — labours to exhaustion. Leadership in the church is recognised by service, not claimed by status. Those who serve sacrificially are the ones to follow.

scripture.text: I rejoice at the coming of Stephanas, Fortunatus, and Achaicus; for that which was lacking on your part, they supplied.
scripture.understanding: Stephanas, Fortunatus and Achaicus had come from Corinth to Paul in Ephesus — very possibly carrying the Corinthians' letter of 7:1. Their παρουσία — presence, coming — made Paul glad, for they ἀναπληρόω — filled up — what was ὑστέρημα, lacking. Fortunatus and Achaicus may have been freedmen or slaves; their names are common slave names. Status did not matter. Their presence did.

scripture.text: For they refreshed my spirit and yours. Therefore acknowledge those who are like that.
scripture.understanding: They ἀναπαύω — refreshed, gave rest to — Paul's spirit, and the Corinthians' too. The same word Jesus uses in Matthew 11:28: “I will give you rest.” Some believers are like a cool drink to everyone they visit. “Therefore ἐπιγινώσκω — recognise, acknowledge, honour — such people.”

scripture.text: The assemblies of Asia greet you. Aquila and Priscilla greet you much in the Lord, together with the assembly that is in their house.
scripture.understanding: The churches of Asia — the Roman province around Ephesus — send ἀσπάζομαι, greetings. And Aquila and Priscilla, Paul's old tentmaking partners from Corinth itself (Acts 18:2–3), greet them warmly, “together with the ἐκκλησία that is in their house.” For the first three centuries, Christians met mainly in homes. Wherever this couple moved — Rome, Corinth, Ephesus, Rome again — a church met in their house.

scripture.text: All the brothers greet you. Greet one another with a holy kiss.
scripture.understanding: “Greet one another with a φίλημα ἅγιον — a holy kiss.” A kiss on the cheek was a common greeting between family members. In the church it expressed that believers — slaves and free, Jews and Greeks, rich and poor — were one family. For a church torn by factions, it was a command to embody reconciliation in the most physical, personal way.

scripture.text: This greeting is by me, Paul, with my own hand.
scripture.understanding: Paul usually dictated his letters to a scribe (Romans 16:22). Here he takes the pen himself: “by me, Paul, with my own χείρ — hand.” His personal signature authenticated the letter (compare 2 Thessalonians 3:17; Galatians 6:11; Colossians 4:18). Imagine the Corinthians seeing the change in handwriting as the letter was read aloud.

scripture.text: If any man doesn’t love the Lord Jesus Christ, let him be accursed. Come, Lord!
scripture.understanding: In his own hand, two of the sharpest words in the letter. “If anyone does not φιλέω — love, have affection for — the Lord, let him be ἀνάθεμα” — accursed, devoted to destruction. The test of true faith is not gifts, knowledge or eloquence. It is love for Jesus. Then an Aramaic phrase, left untranslated in a Greek letter: μαρανα θα — Maranatha. Divided one way, it means ‘Our Lord, come!’; divided another, ‘Our Lord has come.’ The prayer of Revelation 22:20, “come, Lord Jesus,” strongly favours the first. Its survival in Aramaic shows that the earliest Aramaic-speaking believers were already praying to Jesus as Lord.

scripture.text: The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with you.
scripture.understanding: The letter that began with grace (1:3–4) ends with grace. After all the rebukes, Paul's final blessing is not a threat but χάρις — the undeserved favour of the Lord Jesus, which is the only thing that could ever heal Corinth.

scripture.text: My love to all of you in Christ Jesus. Amen.
scripture.understanding: Paul's last line is unique among his letters: “My ἀγάπη to all of you in Christ Jesus.” All of you — including the factions, the proud, the immoral, the litigants, the ones who despised him. Love is not only what Paul commanded in this letter; it is what he gave in it. A father's correction and a father's love were one thing.

visualMeditations.title: The Coin Box on the First Day
visualMeditations.image: Picture a Corinthian believer's home on a Sunday — the first day of the week, the day of the resurrection. Before he goes to the gathering in Gaius' house, a dockworker opens a small wooden box under his bed and drops in a few coins from the week's wages. It is not much. But last week he did the same, and the week before. Across the city, a merchant's wife does the same with a larger sum, a slave with a single small coin. Months later, the boxes are brought together. Men the church trusts are chosen to carry the money across the sea to Jerusalem, to Jewish believers they have never met, who are hungry. And Paul calls the money χάρις — grace.
visualMeditations.meaning: Paul places this instruction right after the triumphant end of chapter 15: “your labor is not in vain in the Lord.” The resurrection makes money matter, because what is given to the Lord is never lost. Notice the pattern of giving: on the first day of the week — connected to worship and the resurrection; each one — every believer, not just the wealthy; set aside and store up — planned, regular, intentional; as he may prosper — in proportion to what God has given. And handled with integrity: people the church approves, with letters, so that no one could question the money. Generous, systematic giving to meet real needs across cultural lines is not a distraction from spiritual life. It is resurrection faith with its wallet open.

visualMeditations.title: The Door and the Lions
visualMeditations.image: Picture Ephesus in the spring: the great temple of Artemis gleaming above the city, the theatre carved into the hillside, crowds of pilgrims, magicians, merchants and silversmiths selling shrines. In a lecture hall Paul has borrowed, he has been teaching every day for two years, and the word has spread through the whole province of Asia (Acts 19:9–10). People are burning their books of magic. And in the shadows, the silversmiths' guild is counting its losses and talking about a riot. Paul writes: a great and effective door has opened to me — and there are many adversaries.
visualMeditations.meaning: Notice the little word “and.” Paul does not say the door is open but there are adversaries. He says both are true together, and he stays. Many believers assume that if God opens a door, it will be easy to walk through; and if opposition comes, the door must have closed. Paul's experience was the opposite. The greatest opportunities often come with the fiercest resistance, because the enemy does not waste his effort on closed doors. Of course, opposition alone does not prove God is in something. But it does not prove He isn't. A year later, the same man would walk away from an open door at Troas because his heart was heavy for this very church (2 Corinthians 2:12–13). Discerning doors takes prayer. But never let adversaries alone convince you that God has closed what He opened.

visualMeditations.title: The Hand That Took the Pen
visualMeditations.image: Picture the scene in Ephesus as the letter is finished. Paul has been dictating for days — perhaps weeks — to a scribe, sentence by sentence, through fifteen chapters of rebuke, instruction, theology and pleading. Now the scribe hands him the pen. Paul's own handwriting, perhaps larger and rougher than the scribe's (compare Galatians 6:11), fills the last lines. And in Corinth months later, as the letter is read aloud in Gaius' house, the reader pauses. He holds it up so they can see the different hand. Then he reads Paul's own words: a solemn warning, an Aramaic prayer, a blessing of grace, and a last line no other letter of his ends with: “My love to all of you in Christ Jesus.”
visualMeditations.meaning: After all the correction — factions, immorality, lawsuits, idolatry, disorder, denial of the resurrection — the last word in Paul's own hand is love. Not love for the faction that liked him; love for all of them. That is how the letter's two halves fit together: the rebukes were love, and the love was not soft. And the warning of verse 22 shows what all of it was for: “If any man doesn’t love the Lord Jesus Christ, let him be accursed.” The final test of a Christian is not giftedness, knowledge or eloquence. It is love for Jesus. And the final prayer is Maranatha — ‘Our Lord, come!’ Paul ends the letter the way the whole Bible ends: “Yes, come, Lord Jesus” (Revelation 22:20). Everything in 1 Corinthians is meant to be lived while waiting for Him.

structure.label: The Collection for Jerusalem (v. 1-4)
structure.body: On the first day of every week each believer is to set aside a proportion of income; trusted delegates chosen by the church will carry the gift to Jerusalem, perhaps with Paul.

structure.label: Paul's Travel Plans (v. 5-9)
structure.body: Paul plans to come through Macedonia and perhaps winter in Corinth, but will stay in Ephesus until Pentecost, because a great door has opened and there are many adversaries.

structure.label: Timothy and Apollos (v. 10-12)
structure.body: Receive Timothy without intimidating him, for he does the Lord's work; Paul urged Apollos to come, but he will come when the time is right.

structure.label: Final Commands (v. 13-14)
structure.body: Watch, stand firm in the faith, be courageous, be strong — and let everything be done in love.

structure.label: Honour Faithful Servants (v. 15-18)
structure.body: Submit to servants like the household of Stephanas, who devoted themselves to serving the saints, and recognise those like Stephanas, Fortunatus and Achaicus who refreshed Paul's spirit.

structure.label: Greetings, Warning and Blessing (v. 19-24)
structure.body: Greetings from Asia, Aquila, Priscilla and the house church; greet one another with a holy kiss; in his own hand Paul pronounces a curse on anyone who does not love the Lord, prays Maranatha, and closes with grace and his love for all.

sections.heading: From the Resurrection to the Offering Box
paragraphs: It can feel like an anticlimax. Chapter 15 soars to the heights of resurrection hope — “Death is swallowed up in victory” — and chapter 16 opens with fundraising. But that transition is the point. Paul has just written, “be steadfast, immovable, always abounding in the Lord’s work, because you know that your labor is not in vain in the Lord” (15:58). The very next sentence is about money. Resurrection faith does not float above practical life. It reaches into the wallet. If what is given to the Lord is never wasted, then generous giving is one of the most reasonable things a resurrection people can do.

The collection was one of Paul's great projects during these years. The church in Jerusalem was poor — possibly because of famine (Acts 11:28–30), persecution, and the economic marginalisation of Jewish believers. Paul gathered gifts from his largely Gentile churches in Galatia, Macedonia and Achaia to relieve them. He explains the theology in Romans 15:27: “if the Gentiles have been made partakers of their spiritual things, they owe it to them also to serve them in fleshly things.” The collection was more than charity; it was a visible demonstration that Jews and Gentiles were one body in Christ. A church that had been divided along social lines at the Lord's Table was now invited to give across ethnic lines to people they had never met.

Verses 2 and 3 give a pattern for Christian giving that is still instructive. It was weekly: “On the first day of the week” — the day of the resurrection, and one of the earliest references to Christians meeting on Sunday (compare Acts 20:7). It was universal: “each one of you.” It was planned: “save,” set aside and store up, not a last-minute response to an emotional appeal. It was proportional: “as he may prosper.” And it was handled with transparent integrity: the church itself chose trusted delegates, who carried letters of introduction (v. 3). Paul would write later, “Having regard for honorable things, not only in the sight of the Lord, but also in the sight of men” (2 Corinthians 8:21). In 2 Corinthians 8 and 9 he will develop the theme at length, including the principle that “God loves a cheerful giver” (9:7). Money is not a separate subject from the gospel. It is one of the clearest places where the gospel shows.

sections.heading: Open Doors, Opposition and the Workers Who Carry the Work
paragraphs: Paul's travel plans in verses 5 to 9 are ordinary and human: he hopes to visit, maybe to winter there, but “if the Lord permits.” He holds his plans loosely under God's sovereignty, as James urges: “you ought to say, ‘If the Lord wills, we will both live, and do this or that’” (James 4:15). And these very plans would later change, prompting the Corinthians to accuse him of fickleness — an accusation he answers in 2 Corinthians 1:15–24. But verse 9 contains a principle that every believer needs: “a great and effective door has opened to me, and there are many adversaries.” The opportunity and the opposition came together. Acts 19 describes what that looked like in Ephesus: extraordinary miracles, people burning magic books worth fifty thousand pieces of silver, and then a riot instigated by silversmiths whose shrine business was collapsing.

Verses 10 to 12 give a glimpse of Paul's co-workers. Timothy is coming, and Paul writes to protect him: “see that he is with you without fear... let no one despise him” (vv. 10–11). Timothy was young and apparently timid, and later letters show Paul encouraging him not to be intimidated (1 Timothy 4:12; 2 Timothy 1:7). A proud, gift-obsessed church like Corinth could easily have looked down on a young, unimpressive messenger. Paul insists that Timothy does the Lord's work “as I also do.” And then Apollos: Paul strongly urged him to visit, but Apollos was unwilling at that time (v. 12). This one verse shows that the factions in Corinth did not reflect any rivalry between the leaders. Paul wanted the very man some Corinthians preferred to him to go to them, and Apollos seems to have stayed away precisely to avoid fuelling the faction that used his name.

Verses 15 to 18 honour the faithful servants who often go unnoticed. The household of Stephanas, the first converts in Achaia, “set themselves to serve the saints” (v. 15). No one appointed them; they appointed themselves to serve. Paul asks the church to submit to such people and to everyone who works and labours (v. 16). Christian leadership is not a title that confers authority; it is recognised in those who serve. Then he names three men who travelled from Corinth to Ephesus — Stephanas, Fortunatus and Achaicus — and says they “refreshed my spirit and yours” (v. 18). Fortunatus and Achaicus may well have been slaves or freedmen; their names were typical of that class. In a church obsessed with status, Paul gives public honour to people whose only credential was faithful, refreshing service. “Therefore acknowledge those who are like that.”

sections.heading: Watch, Stand, Be Strong — and Do It All in Love
paragraphs: Verses 13 and 14 are the letter's final summary, and they come in two parts that must be held together. First, four rapid military commands: “Watch! Stand firm in the faith! Be courageous! Be strong!” (v. 13). Γρηγορεῖτε — stay awake, be alert, the word Jesus used in Gethsemane (Matthew 26:41). Στήκετε ἐν τῇ πίστει — stand firm, hold your ground in the faith, like soldiers holding a line. Ἀνδρίζεσθε — act with courage, the word used in the Greek Old Testament's charge to Joshua to “be strong and courageous.” Κραταιοῦσθε — be strengthened. After everything Corinth had done — divisions, compromise, confusion about basic truths — they needed vigilance, stability and courage, not more spiritual excitement.

But then immediately: “Let all that you do be done in love” (v. 14). Strength without love becomes harshness. Courage without love becomes arrogance. Firmness without love becomes rigidity. Paul will not let the church hear the military commands without the command that governs them. And the phrase is all-encompassing: “all that you do.” This one verse summarises the entire letter. Every issue Paul has addressed — factions, discipline, lawsuits, marriage, idol food, head coverings, the Lord's Supper, spiritual gifts — is finally a question of love. It is chapter 13 compressed into a single sentence, and it is the lens through which everything else in 1 Corinthians is to be read and lived.

Then Paul takes the pen from his scribe and writes the final lines himself (v. 21). The first thing he writes in his own hand is shocking: “If any man doesn’t love the Lord Jesus Christ, let him be accursed” (v. 22). He uses φιλέω here, the warmer word for affection — the same word Jesus used when He asked Peter on the beach whether he loved Him (John 21:15–17). The ultimate test of genuine Christianity is not gifts or knowledge but love for Jesus. Then an Aramaic phrase, μαρανα θα, preserved untranslated in a Greek letter to a Greek church — almost certainly ‘Our Lord, come!’ It appears again in one of the earliest Christian worship manuals outside the New Testament, the Didache, in a prayer connected to the Lord's Supper, and it parallels the Bible's final prayer: “Yes, come, Lord Jesus” (Revelation 22:20). Its survival shows that the earliest Aramaic-speaking church prayed to Jesus as Lord. And the letter ends with grace — “The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with you” — and with a line unique in Paul's letters: “My love to all of you in Christ Jesus.” All of you. After sixteen chapters of correction, the last word is love.

ntConnection.heading: New Testament Connection
paragraphs: The collection Paul organises in verses 1 to 4 runs as a thread through his later letters and Acts. In Romans he explains its purpose: “I am going to Jerusalem, serving the saints. For it has been the good pleasure of Macedonia and Achaia to make a certain contribution for the poor among the saints who are at Jerusalem... For if the Gentiles have been made partakers of their spiritual things, they owe it to them also to serve them in fleshly things” (Romans 15:25–27). In 2 Corinthians 8 and 9 he devotes two whole chapters to encouraging the Corinthians to complete what they had begun, grounding it in the grace of Christ, who “though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor” (2 Corinthians 8:9), and in the principle that “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7). And in Acts, before Felix, Paul says, “after some years, I came to bring gifts for the needy to my nation, and offerings” (Acts 24:17). The coins dropped into boxes in Corinth on the first day of the week reached Jerusalem.

The final commands of verse 13 echo throughout the New Testament. Jesus told His disciples in Gethsemane to “Watch and pray, that you don’t enter into temptation” (Matthew 26:41). Paul tells the Ephesians, “be strong in the Lord, and in the strength of his might. Put on the whole armor of God, that you may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil” (Ephesians 6:10–11). Peter writes, “Be sober and self-controlled. Be watchful. Your adversary, the devil, walks around like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour. Withstand him steadfast in your faith” (1 Peter 5:8–9). And Paul encourages the young and timid Timothy: “For God didn’t give us a spirit of fear, but of power, love, and self-control” (2 Timothy 1:7) — power and love together, exactly the pairing of verses 13 and 14.

And the Aramaic cry of verse 22, Maranatha, is answered in the last words of the Bible. The risen Christ says, “Yes, I come quickly,” and the church replies, “Amen! Yes, come, Lord Jesus” (Revelation 22:20). Paul's personal signature, too, links this letter to his others: “The greeting of me, Paul, with my own hand, which is the sign in every letter” (2 Thessalonians 3:17); “See with what large letters I write to you with my own hand” (Galatians 6:11); “The salutation of me, Paul, with my own hand: remember my bonds. Grace be with you” (Colossians 4:18). In every letter the last word in his own hand is grace. In this one he adds love. The pastor who had corrected Corinth so sharply wanted them to know, in his own handwriting, that he loved every one of them.

lexicon.insight: Strong's: “a contribution.” The word appears only in these two verses in the New Testament. Outside the Bible it was used for special collections, sometimes for religious purposes or taxes. Paul never uses the ordinary word for money when describing this project. Elsewhere he calls it χάρις, grace (v. 3; 2 Corinthians 8:4, 6–7), κοινωνία, fellowship (2 Corinthians 8:4; 9:13), διακονία, service (2 Corinthians 8:4; 9:1), and εὐλογία, blessing (2 Corinthians 9:5). The vocabulary itself is a theology of giving. A financial gift for brothers in need is grace in action, fellowship made visible, service rendered to Christ and a blessing that flows both ways.

Strong's: “a portal or entrance (the opening or the closure, literally or figuratively).” Paul uses an open door as his image for a God-given opportunity to preach the gospel — here, at Troas (2 Corinthians 2:12), and in his prayer request to the Colossians: “that God may open to us a door for the word” (Colossians 4:3). In Acts 14:27 God “had opened a door of faith to the nations.” The risen Christ tells the church in Philadelphia, “I have set before you an open door, which no one can shut” (Revelation 3:8). The important truth in verse 9 is that God's open doors are often surrounded by adversaries. The opposition does not shut what God has opened.

Strong's: “to keep awake, i.e. watch (literally or figuratively).” It is the word Jesus used repeatedly when warning His disciples to be ready for His return: “Watch therefore, for you don’t know in what hour your Lord comes” (Matthew 24:42), and in Gethsemane, “Watch and pray, that you don’t enter into temptation” (Matthew 26:41). Paul uses it in 1 Thessalonians 5:6 — “let’s watch and be sober.” The command is to spiritual alertness: refusing to drift, to fall asleep in comfort, to be caught off guard by temptation or false teaching. Corinth had been dozing — some had even been drunk at the Lord's Table. Paul's first final command is: wake up and stay awake.

Strong's: “to act manly.” This is the only occurrence of the word in the New Testament. It comes from ἀνήρ, man, and in Greek culture it meant to show courage, to act bravely, to face danger without shrinking. In the Greek Old Testament it appears in the repeated charge to Joshua: “Be strong and courageous” (Joshua 1:6–7, 9), and in Psalm 27:14 and 31:24. Paul is not addressing only men; the whole church is commanded. And the courage he means is not bravado. It is the steady nerve to stand firm in the faith when it is unpopular, to hold the truth when others drift, to endure opposition without retreat. And it must always be followed by verse 14: courage, done in love.

Strong's: “maranatha, i.e. an exclamation of the approaching divine judgment.” It is an Aramaic phrase written in Greek letters, and can be divided as marana tha, ‘Our Lord, come!’, or maran atha, ‘Our Lord has come.’ The prayer of Revelation 22:20 — “Yes, come, Lord Jesus” — strongly suggests the first. Its presence in a Greek letter to a Gentile church shows that it had become a fixed part of Christian worship, carried over from the very first Aramaic-speaking believers in Jerusalem. That is historically significant: within the first generation, Jewish believers were praying to Jesus as “our Lord” — an address only appropriate to God. Maranatha is the heartbeat of the church between the resurrection and the return: Lord, come.

holySpiritRevelation.intro: The Spirit is dealing with three things in this chapter: whether your resurrection faith has reached your wallet, whether opposition has convinced you that God has closed a door He opened, and whether love is the root of everything you do.

items.title: Resurrection Faith With an Open Wallet
items.body: Paul moves straight from “your labor is not in vain in the Lord” to “On the first day of the week, let each one of you save.” The Spirit is asking whether your belief in the resurrection has reached your money. Do you give regularly, intentionally and proportionally — or only when moved by an appeal? Do you give across lines of culture and distance to brothers and sisters you have never met? Is your giving grace — a joyful response to the grace you have received — or a reluctant tax? If Christ is risen, nothing given to Him is lost. Ask Him today what He wants you to set aside, and start this first day of the week.

items.title: The Door Is Still Open
items.body: You stepped through a door God opened — a ministry, a calling, a relationship, a work — and then the adversaries came. Criticism, resistance, spiritual attack, discouragement. And you have begun to wonder whether you misread God, whether the door has closed. The Spirit wants you to see verse 9 again: “a great and effective door has opened to me, and there are many adversaries.” Both at once. Opposition is not proof that God is absent. Often it is evidence that you are standing in exactly the place the enemy does not want you to be. Pray for discernment, and seek counsel. But do not let the adversaries alone persuade you to walk away from what God has opened.

items.title: Is Love the Root?
items.body: “Let all that you do be done in love.” All. Your service, your correction of others, your theology, your giving, your work, your parenting, your worship, your conversations online. The Spirit is asking whether love is the root of what you do, or whether it has been replaced by duty, pride, fear, competition or habit. And verse 22 gives the deepest form of the question: do you love the Lord Jesus? Not just believe in Him, serve Him or know about Him — love Him, with the warm affection of φιλέω. If that love has grown cold, do not try to manufacture it. Go back to the cross and the empty tomb, and let Him love you again. Then pray the church's oldest prayer: Maranatha.

audit.title: The Giving Check
audit.body: Look at your giving over the last three months. Is it regular (weekly or monthly)? Is it planned in advance? Is it proportional to what God has given you? Does any of it reach believers in need beyond your own church and culture? Write down one change you will make.

audit.title: The Door Check
audit.body: Is there an opportunity you have pulled back from because of opposition? Write it down. Then ask honestly: did God close this door, or did I let the adversaries close it? Who could I ask for wise counsel about it?

audit.title: The Refreshing Check
audit.body: Stephanas, Fortunatus and Achaicus “refreshed my spirit.” Who in your life refreshes you? Have you acknowledged them? And who would say you refresh them? If no one comes to mind, ask what it would take for you to become that kind of believer.

practices.title: A First-Day Offering
practices.body: This coming Sunday, before you leave for church, set aside a specific amount for the Lord — planned, proportional and prayed over. Do it the same way every first day of the week for the next month. In addition, choose one ministry that serves believers in poverty or persecution in another part of the world, and give a gift to it this month. As you give, pray: “Lord, this is grace. Because Christ is risen, my labour — and my giving — is not in vain in You.”

practices.title: Honouring a Stephanas
practices.body: Think of one person in your church who has quietly “set themselves to serve the saints” — not because of a title, but because they saw a need and filled it. This week, acknowledge them as verse 18 commands: tell them specifically how they have refreshed you, thank them publicly if appropriate, and ask how you could share their load. Then close the week by praying the last words of this letter over your church, aloud: “Maranatha. The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with you. My love to all of you in Christ Jesus.”

prayerReflection: “Lord Jesus, You are risen, and my labour is not in vain in You. So I give You my money, my plans, my doors and my heart. Teach me to give on the first day of the week with joy, regularly and generously, as grace returned for grace. Let my giving cross every line that once divided me from my brothers and sisters. Father, thank You for every door You have opened. When adversaries come, do not let me mistake their noise for Your voice. Give me the discernment to know when You have closed a door, and the courage to stay when You have opened one. Make me watchful, firm in the faith, courageous and strong — and let all that I do be done in love. Thank You for the faithful servants who have refreshed my spirit. Help me to honour them, to follow their example, and to become a refreshment to others. Lord, I love You. Not only believe in You, not only serve You — I love You. Where my love has grown cold, warm it again with Your grace. And I join the oldest prayer of Your church: Maranatha. Our Lord, come! Until You do, let Your grace be with me, and let Your love flow through me to all. In the mighty name of Jesus, Amen!”

storyConnections.title: Be Strong and Courageous
storyConnections.summary: After Moses died, the task of leading Israel into the promised land fell on Joshua. Ahead lay the Jordan in flood, fortified cities, and nations stronger than Israel. And God spoke to him three times in nine verses with the same command: be strong and courageous. He promised that no one would stand against Joshua all the days of his life; that as He had been with Moses, He would be with him; that He would not leave or forsake him. And He tied Joshua's courage to the Word: this book of the law was not to depart from his mouth. The Greek Old Testament uses the same verb Paul uses in 1 Corinthians 16:13 for “be courageous.” Joshua's courage was not self-confidence. It was confidence in the God who goes ahead. That is the courage Paul commands: stand firm in the faith, because God is with you.

storyConnections.title: Joseph Stores Up Grain
storyConnections.summary: When Joseph interpreted Pharaoh's dreams, he warned of seven years of plenty followed by seven years of famine, and advised that during the good years a portion of the harvest be set aside and stored in the cities. For seven years, the grain was gathered and stored until it could not be measured. When the famine came, there was bread in Egypt, and people came from every land to buy grain — including Joseph's own brothers. Joseph's plan was steady, proportional and planned in advance, and it saved countless lives, including the family through whom the Messiah would come. Paul's instruction in 1 Corinthians 16:2 follows the same wisdom: set aside regularly, as God prospers you, so that when the need comes, the provision is ready. Systematic generosity is not unspiritual. It is how God feeds the hungry.

storyConnections.title: The Room on the Roof for Elisha
storyConnections.summary: A wealthy woman in Shunem noticed the prophet Elisha passing through her town and urged him to eat with her. Then she said to her husband that this man was a holy man of God, and suggested they build a small room on the roof with a bed, a table, a chair and a lamp, so that he would have a place to rest whenever he came. No one asked her to do it; she set herself to serve. Elisha was refreshed by her hospitality and asked what he could do for her. Through him, God gave her a son, and later raised that son from the dead. Like the household of Stephanas, the Shunammite woman devoted herself to serving God's servants, and her quiet, practical kindness refreshed the man of God. God honoured her far beyond anything she had given.
